text: The Two Fridas (Las dos Fridas in Spanish) is an oil painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, created in 1939 and considered one of her most notable works. It is a double self-portrait depicting two versions of Kahlo seated together: one in a white European-style Victorian dress and the other in a traditional Tehuana dress. The painting was exhibited in January 1940 at the International Surrealist Exhibition in Mexico City alongside The Wounded Table. Kahlo painted it the same year she divorced Diego Rivera, although they remarried a year later. According to her friend Fernando Gamboa, the painting was inspired by two works seen at the Louvre earlier that year: Théodore Chassériau's The Two Sisters and the anonymous Gabrielle d'Estrées and One of Her Sisters. The painting remained in Kahlo's possession until it was acquired by the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes (INBA) in 1947 and transferred to the Museo de Arte Moderno on December 28, 1966, where it is currently housed. Art historians suggest the two figures represent Kahlo's dual heritage: her father, Guillermo Kahlo, was German, and her mother, Matilde Calderon, was Mexican. Another interpretation is that the Tehuana Frida is the one adored by Diego Rivera, while the European Frida is rejected by him. In Frida's own recollection, the image reflects a memory of a childhood imaginary friend. Both Fridas hold items in their laps—the Mexican Frida holds a miniature portrait of Diego Rivera, while the European Frida holds forceps. Blood spills from a broken blood vessel in the European Frida’s dress, which connects the two through a vein running from their hands to their hearts. This alludes to Kahlo’s lifelong pain, surgical procedures, and the Aztec tradition of human sacrifice. Because the painting was completed shortly after her divorce, the European Frida is missing a piece of herself—her Diego. Each Frida has an open heart; the Mexican Frida’s is healthy, while the European Frida’s is open and cut, symbolizing two separate personalities and the constant pain Kahlo endured. The vein connecting them signifies that despite their differences, both figures constitute one Frida. Hispanic studies professor Sarah M. Misemer argues that Kahlo’s multi-racial representation reflects the colonial era’s impact on Mexico’s racial demographics and serves as a cultural symbol for the Mexican nation. The painting inspired a play titled Las Dos Fridas (1998) by Bárbara Córcega, María del Carmen Farías, and Abraham Oceransky, in which two actresses play different versions of Kahlo named Espina (Thorn) and Flor (Flower), representing the same person. Espina wears a Tehuana outfit, while Flor wears a 1940s suit. In the original production, Córcega and Farías played the roles. The play begins with Flor questioning Espina about Kahlo’s identity, with Espina explaining aspects of her gender and career. Historians interpret this as reflecting Kahlo’s multifaceted identity, emphasized by a sketch of her self-portrait on stage. The play features the two versions of Kahlo acting out scenes from her life, focusing on her struggles in her marriage with Rivera, who had numerous affairs with other women. The play addresses the shame Kahlo felt and her denial of Rivera’s infidelities, and highlights how Kahlo used her physical pain to keep Rivera in the relationship, a point supported by Misemer’s research.
